title: SDK ergonomics for resumable fetch, adaptive pagination, and deterministic retries
creator: Miguel Ortega
description: Problem statement: Customers build production features that combine resumed reads (cursored pagination), long-lived streams, and deterministic retries. Current SDK behavior across languages is inconsistent: Python iterator patterns differ from TS async iterators, Go callbacks don't surface resumability uniformly, and retry semantics can reorder events or duplicate side-effects. This ticket defines an ergonomic, language-idiomatic contract for: resumable fetch (cursor + stable offsets), adaptive pagination (windowed fetching with prefetch/backpressure), deterministic retry semantics for idempotent vs non-idempotent operations, and streaming iterators that gracefully degrade when server-side framing changes.
background: Multiple customer support cases and internal infra incidents show edge cases where clients resume after transient failures and either lose items, receive duplicates, or observe non-deterministic ordering. Engineering and DX teams have prototyped adapters per-language; we need a single product-level contract and acceptance criteria so SDK teams can converge without breaking existing consumers.
goals: Define a cross-language contract for resumable fetch semantics and portable cursor encoding
Specify deterministic retry behavior and idempotency token patterns for client-side retry logic
Provide language-specific ergonomics for Python, TypeScript, and Go that feel native to each ecosystem
Ensure graceful streaming degradation and a compatibility policy for adding/removing fields or chunk framing changes
Produce acceptance tests and compatibility test harness to include in CI for each SDK
scope_in: Cursor format recommendation and migration strategy
Client-side deterministic retry algorithm and idempotency guidance
API sketches for Python iterator, TS async iterator, and Go channel-based consumer
Acceptance criteria, test cases, and CI harness definitions
Developer docs and migration notes for existing SDK users
scope_out: Server-side implementation of pagination endpoints (only recommendations provided)
Automated server-side cursor translators for legacy cursors
api_sketches: Python: def fetch_items(cursor=None, page_size=100, prefetch=True) -> Iterator[Item]; supports .resume(cursor) to return stable continuation object
TypeScript: async function listItems(opts): AsyncIterable<Item>; return object exposes getCursor() and resume(cursor) helpers; built-in backpressure via for-await-of and optional prefetch parameter

Go: func ListItems(ctx context.Context, opts ListOptions) (<-chan Item, <-chan error, ResumeToken); consumer reads from channel, receives ResumeToken on close; library provides Resume(ctx, token) helper
acceptance_criteria: Language SDKs expose resume token that is opaque but stable across minor server changes
Resuming a paginated list after a transient network failure returns the same item sequence with no duplicates or gaps for idempotent reads

Deterministic retry behavior: client retries must be safe by default for read/list endpoints; non-idempotent endpoints require explicit idempotency token parameter and SDK must surface utilities to generate and persist tokens
Streaming consumers receive clearly delimited event frames; if server adds optional fields the SDK retains ordering and surfaces new fields in a backwards-compatible manner
Compatibility tests: CI test harness includes at least 12 fuzzed resume/retry scenarios per SDK and all pass
Documentation: migration guide and quickstart examples for each language included in the SDK repo
rollout_plan: Phase 1: Finalize product contract and API sketches (this ticket). Phase 2: Implement prototypes in each SDK repo behind feature flags. Phase 3: Baseline compatibility tests and run on sample customer workloads. Phase 4: Soft-launch SDK changes with opt-in prerelease packages and collect telemetry. Phase 5: Promote to GA and provide migration guides and deprecation schedule for older patterns.
test_plan: Unit tests: cursor encode/decode, resume idempotency asserts
Integration: client+mock-server scenarios for mid-stream disconnects, partial page ACKs, duplicate event injection
Compatibility matrix: server v1/v2 behavior, SDK versions previous/next
Load test: prefetch/backpressure under realistic latency profiles to verify memory bounds
CI: cross-language fuzz harness that replays recorded failure traces
compatibility_policy: Semver for SDK surface: minor releases may add ergonomic helpers but must not change resume token format or retry default semantics. Resume token format is opaque; server may extend token but must provide adapter layer for tokens older than 2 major server versions. Breaking changes require a migration guide and a minimum 3-month overlap with old token format. SDKs must provide opt-out flags for strict mode (throw on unknown fields) vs lenient mode (preserve unknowns).
risks: Opaque resume tokens may be unintelligible to advanced users who want to inspect cursors
Server-side cursor evolution could require complex adapter logic if not versioned carefully
Non-uniform language ergonomics may still leak behavior differences leading to customer confusion
Backpressure/prefetch tuning introduces tradeoffs between latency and memory usage
